newsitem.title: POLAND: GERMANS CHARGED IN POLAND OVER LAND PURCHASES-TV.
newsitem.headline: GERMANS CHARGED IN POLAND OVER LAND PURCHASES-TV.

text.p: Polish prosecutors have charged nine Germans and five Poles allegedly involved in forming front companies to circumvent rules restricting land purchases by foreigners, public television reported on Tuesday.

It said that, according to prosecutors in the northern Szczecin province bordering Germany, the Germans formed fictitious companies with majority Polish capital that bought land at auction from the state treasury's agriculture property agency.
"After the auctions the Poles gave up their shares," the television reported, adding that the Germans had in this way allegedly acquired 20,000 hectares of ground.
Poland fears that so long as its land prices lag behind those in its Western neighbour, wealthy Germans may be able to buy up large tracts of farming land cheaply.

Poland last year partially relaxed rules on selling land and real estate to foreigners to meet conditions for joining the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, but the move aroused strong political controversy.
A new law allowed foreigners to buy apartments and up to 4,000 square metres (4,784 square yards) of urban land without a government permit.
But farm land purchases still require permits from the interior ministry, after approval from the defence and agriculture ministries.
The Szczecin prosecutors were not immediately available to confirm the report or give details.
In April Polish Interior Minister Leszek Miller said the law would not be relaxed again until Poland was in the European Union -- which may not be until 2001 or 2002 at the earliest.
Miller said that in 1996, the ministry granted foreigners 1,414 permits to buy land and as a result 2,400 hectares (5,930 acres) were sold -- mostly to Germans.

The Polish Peasant Party, junior partner of Miller's ex-communists in the ruling coalition, fears that foreigners may be buying land extensively through local proxies and that this will make it too expensive for Polish farmers.
But Polish officials have so far said they had little evidence as to what extent this might be happening. -- Anthony Barker +48 22 653 9700
